prompt: An insurance company charges $\$500$ for a one-year policy. With probability $0.02$ the customer files a claim and the company pays out $\$20{,}000$; otherwise it pays nothing. What is the company's expected profit per policy, in dollars?
hint: Profit is what comes in minus what goes out. The $\$500$ always comes in; the payout only sometimes goes out.

hints.text: Profit is what comes in minus what goes out. The $\$500$ always comes in; the payout only sometimes goes out.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: a $\$10$ ticket pays $\$100$ with probability $0.05$. Expected profit for the seller is $10 - 0.05(100) = 10 - 5 = \$5$. Same structure here.
Expected payout $= 0.02 \times 20{,}000$. Subtract that from the $\$500$ premium.

explanation: Define profit $P$: with probability $0.98$ the company keeps $\$500$; with probability $0.02$ it gets $500 - 20{,}000 = -\$19{,}500$.
So the company expects to earn $\$100$ per policy. On a single policy it may lose big, but averaged over thousands it earns about $\$100$ each.

alternativeExplanations.title: Premium minus expected payout
steps: The payout is a random variable with expected value $0.02 \times 20{,}000 = \$400$ out.
Expected profit $= 500 - 400 = \$100$. Linearity of expectation lets you subtract expected values directly.

alternativeExplanations.title: A thousand policies
steps: About $2\%$, or 20 customers, file claims: payout $= 20 \times 20{,}000 = \$400{,}000$.
